1.pericope_label: Saul hunts David at En-gedi and turns aside into the cave where David is hidden

schools.summary: Henry marks the ingratitude of the pursuit: no sooner had Saul come home safely from chasing the Philistines than he enquired after David to do him a mischief, and it is not enough for Saul that David is cooped up, for he cannot be easy while he is alive. On the cave he allows that covering the feet may mean easing nature but prefers sleep. Of the men’s urging he makes a double warning about misreading God: the Lord had assured David that he would deliver him from Saul, and his men read that as a warrant to destroy Saul; and because it was now in his power to kill him they concluded he might lawfully do it.

Ellicott reads the size of the force as a measure of the fear behind it, three thousand chosen men showing how thoroughly Saul was impressed with David’s power and how plainly he looked on him as a rival king, with the Ziphites, who knew the passes of that barren region, ready to guide him. On the cave he holds the simple sense enough: fatigued with the morning’s march the king withdrew about midday for a siesta and an attendant threw the royal mantle lightly over his feet, the other reading by no means suiting a narrative in which time was needed for a sentinel to inform David and for David to approach, cut the hem and retire. He adds that these caverns are as dark as midnight and the keenest eye cannot see four paces inward, while one long inside and looking out can observe all that passes, so David could watch Saul come in while Saul saw only impenetrable darkness. He has David listen to the tempter for a moment only, until the thought passed through his soul that the sleeping man was the anointed of Jehovah, whom he, himself an anointed king, could not touch. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the rocks of the wild goats is probably no proper name but a general term for the rocks of that locality, from the number of wild goats and chamois found all over the region; and on the alleged promise they allow that the words might refer to an oracle received through a prophet but hold that what follows shows David had received none, the men having treated the leadings of providence as a divine intimation and called that a word of Jehovah.

Clarke thinks the Philistine business had been slight, probably only a small marauding party on the Israelitish borders, soon suppressed. On the name of the rocks he reports the versions at variance: the Vulgate paraphrases them as the most precipitous rocks over which the ibexes alone can travel, the Targum makes them the caverns of the rocks, and the Greek turns the phrase into a proper name, evidently a corruption of the Hebrew. Of the cave he takes covering the feet of easing nature, with the Vulgate, the Greek, the Targum and the Arabic, after which the king lay down to repose; and he relays the rabbinic conceit that God caused a spider to weave her web over the cave’s mouth so that Saul took it for granted no one had lately been there, calling it one of the most elegant traditions in their whole collection. He goes further than the rest on David’s intention, judging from the circumstances that he rose meaning to take Saul’s life and was prevented only by the remonstrance of God in his conscience. Wesley adds that the rocks are exceeding steep and dangerous to travellers, as an eye-witness has left on record, and yet Saul was so transported with rage as to venture himself and his army there; and he argues the siesta from the man, since Saul was a soldier used to sleeping on the ground who, weary with incessant marching, both needed and desired rest, God so disposing him that David might have this occasion to demonstrate his integrity.

debates.question: What did Saul go into the cave to do?

positions.view: To ease nature, with the Vulgate, the Greek, the Targum and the Arabic, lying down to rest afterwards
To sleep: fatigued with the march he withdrew for a midday siesta, which alone leaves time for what follows
To sleep, as a soldier used to the ground and weary with incessant marching
Either reading is possible, but sleep is the more probable

debates.question: Did David rise intending to kill Saul?

positions.view: Yes: the circumstances indicate it, and that is why his heart smote him — he was prevented by the remonstrance of God in his conscience
He listened to the tempter for a moment only, until the thought of the anointing stopped him
His men mistook both the promises and the providences of God; David did not

outliers.claim: Alone in using the optics of the cave — blinding darkness looking in, clear sight looking out — as the physical ground of the whole episode.
Alone in holding that David actually rose with the intention of killing Saul, and alone in preserving the rabbinic tale of the spider’s web over the cave mouth.

themes: Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi
Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel… upon the rocks of the wild goats
And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet
Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand
Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily

5.pericope_label: David’s heart smites him, and he restrains his men from touching the Lord’s anointed

schools.summary: Ellicott says the conscience struck not for what David had done to Saul but for the momentary thought that had stained his soul, of slaying the Lord’s anointed; he prefers this to the view of Clericus, that David feared Saul would take the sign in bad part, and holds there is no sign at all of David’s regretting that he cut the fringe. He notes that the act was severely judged elsewhere, a rabbi reading the cutting of the robe as the slighting of clothes that would one day leave David himself unwarmed by them, and calls it one of those cryptographs whose real lesson is reverence for the guides of Israel, here represented by Saul. Keil and Delitzsch take the opposite view of the conscience, that it reproached him because he regarded the cutting itself as an injury done to the king; and they observe that the firmness of the refusal shows clearly enough that no word of Jehovah had come to him to do as he liked with Saul.

Henry stands with Keil and Delitzsch on the conscience: though it did Saul no real hurt, and served David afterwards for proof that it had been in his power to kill him, because it was an affront to royal dignity he wished he had not done it; and he draws the general lesson that it is a good thing to have a heart within us smiting us for sins that seem little, since it is a sign that conscience is awake and tender and will prevent greater sins. He notices what David refused to consider: not Saul as his enemy, the one man standing in the way of his preferment, for then he would have been induced to hearken to the temptation, but Saul as God’s anointed, under the particular protection of the divine law, and as his master, to whom he owed faithfulness. On the restraining of the men he presses the double refusal, that David would not do this evil thing himself nor suffer those about him to do it, and so rendered good for evil to the man from whom he had received evil for good, being herein both a type of Christ, who saved his persecutors, and an example to all Christians to overcome evil with good.

Clarke grounds the refusal in the anointing: however unworthily Saul was acting, he had been appointed to his office by God and could be removed only by the authority that placed him there, so that the Lord’s anointed is sacred as to his person in the Lord’s sight. It is an awful thing to kill a king, he adds, even the most untoward, once constitutionally appointed; no experiment of the kind has ever succeeded, and had David taken away Saul’s life he would in God’s sight have been a murderer. The restraining of the men he makes a duty rather than a kindness, since as David could restrain them it was his duty to do so, and had he connived at their killing him he would himself have been the murderer; and he adds that in praying for the king we call God the only Ruler of princes, their authority being the highest among men and next to God’s own, quoting the poet that kings are supreme over their subjects while Jove is supreme over kings.

Gill puts the conscience plainly, that it accused him and he repented of what he had done. Of the restraining he reports the manner with the Targum, that David pacified his men and made them easy in his not having slain the king, reconciling their minds by observing that Saul was the anointed of the Lord.

debates.question: Why did David’s heart smite him?

positions.view: For the momentary thought of slaying the Lord’s anointed, not for the cutting; there is no sign he regretted that
For the cutting itself, which he regarded as an injury done to the king
For the cutting, as an affront to royal dignity, though it did Saul no real hurt

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the episode into a standing constitutional maxim against regicide, and in holding that restraining others was itself a duty whose neglect would have made David a murderer.
Alone in reporting a rabbinic tradition that condemns the cutting of the robe outright, against the chapter’s own estimate of the act.

themes: And it came to pass afterward, that David’s heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt
The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord’s anointed
So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul

8.pericope_label: David calls after Saul and pleads his innocence from the mouth of the cave

schools.summary: Ellicott has the outlaw let the king proceed some little way before calling after him, with an address of the deepest reverence and an act of the profoundest homage an inferior could pay a superior, since he would show Saul at least that he was no rival king. He supplies the enemies behind the slanders: David had many deadly foes at court who laboured with success to deepen Saul’s jealousy, Doeg among the most prominent, another the Benjamite named in the title of the seventh psalm, with the Ziphites represented there too. He denies that father here means father-in-law, since the king’s daughter had probably already been given to another man, taking it for the reverence of the young to the old and of the loyal subject to the sovereign. He flags a crux in one clause, since the literal rendering would make Jehovah himself bid David kill, defended by some who treat God’s allowing Saul to choose that cavern as a direction to slay him, though the English rightly follows the Syriac and Chaldee in supplying some, or better one. On the proverb he gathers from Clericus and Grotius that actions usually correspond to the quality of the mind, and adds the Greek saying that from a bad raven comes a bad egg; and he observes that the original of the second simile is stronger still, a single flea, which is not easily caught and if caught is poor game for a royal hunter. Keil and Delitzsch note that David called out so that, when the king looked round, he might expostulate with him in words at once reverent and earnest, sharpening his conscience as to the unfounded nature of his suspicion; and they give the proverb’s force in a sentence, that only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself, and David does not.

Henry finds courage in the mere showing of his head, since David had reason to think Saul would be the death of him as soon as he saw him, yet he laid that jealousy aside and bowed, teaching us to order ourselves reverently even to superiors who have injured us. He calls it a piece of respect due to crowned heads, if they do amiss, to charge it upon those about them, and notes that David had reason enough to think Saul persecuted him purely from his own envy, yet courteously supposes that others put him on to it. He puts the evidence at its sharpest: had the charge been true David would now have had Saul’s head in his hand and not the skirt of his robe, for he could as easily have cut off the one as the other. Of the proverb he allows a second sense, that men’s own iniquity will ruin them at last, and draws the rule that though wickedness proceed from the wicked it must not proceed from us by way of retaliation, since though the dog bark at the sheep the sheep does not bark at the dog.

Gill sees the purpose of the complaint about men’s words, that David laid the blame on the courtiers rather than on Saul the rather to reconcile him and make him willing to listen. Of the address he keeps both senses, a father naturally as having married his daughter and civilly as a king who ought to have been the father of his country. On the proverb he asks instead whose it is, reporting Kimchi for the first man and the Talmud for the Ancient of days.
Clarke notes on the two similes that a dead dog was a term of the most sovereign contempt, the Targum rendering both figures as one weak and one contemptible.

debates.question: In what sense does David call Saul his father?

positions.view: Not as father-in-law, the king’s daughter having probably already been given to another; it is the reverence of the young to the old and of subject to sovereign
In both senses: naturally, as having married his daughter, and civilly, as a king who ought to be the father of his country

debates.question: What does the proverb of the ancients mean?

positions.view: That actions correspond to the quality of the mind — had David conspired, the deed would have followed
That only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself, and David does not
Either that men’s own iniquity ruins them at last, or that bad men do bad things — and in neither case may we retaliate
The question is rather whose proverb it is: Kimchi assigns it to the first man, the Talmud to the Ancient of days

outliers.claim: Alone in treating the clause about who bade David kill as a textual crux, and in showing why the literal rendering would put the counsel in God’s own mouth.
Alone in asking who the ancients of the proverb were rather than what the proverb means.

themes: David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave, and cried after Saul, saying, My lord the king
Wherefore hearest thou men’s words, saying, Behold, David seeketh thy hurt?
Moreover, my father, see, yea, see the skirt of thy robe in my hand
As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked
After whom is the king of Israel come out? after a dead dog, after a flea

16.pericope_label: Saul weeps, owns David the more righteous, and binds him by oath to spare his seed

schools.summary: Gill finds it wonderful that Saul, so eager for David’s life, should stand still and not fall upon him, and ascribes it to the restraining providence of God, to his surprise at David coming out of the cave, and above all to the skirt in his hand, a sure token that his life had been spared. On the confession he reaches the same verdict as Henry: Saul still thought himself righteous, and though David’s righteousness was so glaring that his enemy himself being judge acknowledged it, he would not confess his own wickedness, having no true sense of sin. Of the certainty about the kingdom he adds a token, that the cutting of the skirt might have recalled the rending of Samuel’s mantle, with a Jewish tradition that Samuel had told Saul the man who cut off his skirt should reign after him. He follows the keeping of the oath, in the sparing of Mephibosheth and the punishing of Ishbosheth’s murderers.

Henry agrees that God restrained him, supposes Saul struck with amazement at the singularity of the event, and says his heart must have been harder than a stone if this had not affected him. He measures the confession exactly: Saul should have said, Thou art righteous but I am wicked, whereas the utmost he will own is that David is the more righteous, and bad men commonly go no further, allowing that others are better than they; many mourn for their sins, he adds, who do not truly repent of them, weeping bitterly yet continuing in league with them. He observes that David had the better claim to such an oath and did not press it, and that Saul, who had ruined his own soul and never took care to prevent that ruin, was nonetheless very solicitous that his name should not be cut off. He closes on the parting: Saul went home convinced but not converted, ashamed of his envy yet keeping that root of bitterness, and God has many ways to tie the hands of persecutors when he does not turn their hearts.

Clarke reads the address as the measure of the change, since David had called Saul his master, lord and king, and Saul accosts him as his son, to show he wished to receive him as formerly into his family. On the certainty about the kingdom he states the indictment in a line, that Saul knew this before and yet pursued him with the most deadly hatred. On the oath he notes the asymmetry, that Saul knew an oath would bind David though it had not bound himself, having sworn to Jonathan that David should not be slain and yet sought by every means to destroy him. Wesley says David would trust him no more, having had frequent experience of his inconstancy.

Ellicott reports Clericus, that from such magnanimity Saul concluded a man so superior in soul to kings could not but reign, and calls it a good comment with more behind it: Saul had never forgotten Samuel’s word that the kingdom was rent from him and given to a better neighbour, whom the son of Jesse’s bright career seemed to point out. He explains the request about the seed from the practice of the jealous East, where a new dynasty commonly destroyed the fallen house, a fate Jonathan had dreaded enough to write into his own covenant with David. Keil and Delitzsch judge the wish perfectly sincere, David’s behaviour having conquered for the moment the evil demon of Saul’s heart; the conviction had long forced itself upon him, and drove the persecution whenever the evil spirit had the upper hand.

debates.question: How far does Saul’s confession go?

positions.view: Not far: he should have said he was wicked, and owns only that David is the more righteous — the usual limit of bad men’s confessions
The comparison itself shows he still thought himself righteous and had no true sense of sin
It was sincere while it lasted: David’s conduct had for the moment conquered the evil demon of his heart

debates.question: What made Saul certain David would reign?

positions.view: With Clericus, the magnanimity itself — but behind it Samuel’s word that the kingdom was given to a better neighbour
The cut skirt recalled the rent mantle, and a Jewish tradition made that the very sign
He knew it before, and pursued him with deadly hatred notwithstanding

outliers.claim: Alone in pressing the asymmetry of the oath, that Saul trusted David’s word while having broken his own sworn promise to Jonathan.
Alone in explaining the request for the oath from the dynastic massacres customary in the East, and from Jonathan’s having feared the same fate.

themes: Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept
Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil
For if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away?
I know well that thou shalt surely be king
Swear now therefore unto me by the Lord, that thou wilt not cut off my seed after me
